name: GitLab
description: The DevSecOps platform that puts repos, CI/CD, security scanning and deployment in one app - a serious pick for teams that want everything self-hosted or under one vendor. The money is in selling migrations, managed pipelines and compliance-grade DevOps work around it.
visits: The default self-hostable DevOps platform: 50M+ registered users, single application covering the whole software lifecycle, and the only major git host that ships SAST/DAST in the box. Duo Agent Platform brings AI code review and agentic chat on top.
pricing_details: Verified from about.gitlab.com/pricing (Oct 2026). Free: $0 - 5 users per top-level group, 400 compute minutes/mo, 10 GiB storage, static app security testing included. Premium: $29/user/mo billed annually - unlimited users, 10,000 compute minutes/mo, advanced CI/CD, SLA management, priority support, plus a promotional $12/user/mo of GitLab Credits for AI features. Ultimate: custom pricing - 50,000 compute minutes/mo, full application security testing, supply-chain security, vulnerability management, portfolio and value-stream management, compliance tooling, plus promotional $24/user/mo of credits. AI (Duo Agent Platform: AI code review, agentic chat, code suggestions) is billed through GitLab Credits usage - the old flat-seat Duo Pro ($19/user/mo) and Duo Enterprise ($39/user/mo) add-ons are being replaced by this credit model, and GitLab does not publish a public per-credit price. Paid add-ons: extra Compute Minutes and Storage. Premium and Ultimate can run on gitlab.com, self-managed (your servers), or GitLab Dedicated. A 50-dev org on Premium pays about $17,400/yr before any credit usage.
pros: One application for the whole lifecycle - repos, MRs, CI/CD, registries, security scans and deploy wiring in a single UI, so there is no glue layer of webhooks and third-party dashboards to maintain

Self-managed is a first-class citizen - the same Premium tier runs on your own hardware or GitLab Dedicated, which is exactly what regulated clients (finance, health, government) demand and GitHub cannot sell them as easily
Security scanning ships in the box - SAST on Free, full DAST/dependency/container scanning on Ultimate - instead of a separate product, so compliance stories sell without a second procurement fight

CI config is genuinely powerful: parent-child pipelines, multi-project pipelines, DAG dependencies and needs, downstream includes from a central repo - big orgs run hundreds of pipelines off shared templates

The AI direction is pragmatic - Duo Agent Platform does code review and agentic chat on top of real pipeline infrastructure, and Duo Core is included with Premium/Ultimate rather than another seat upsell (though usage still burns credits)
cons: Per-user pricing gets brutal at scale: 50 developers on Premium is about $17,400/yr, and that is before any GitLab Credits usage for AI features - GitHub Team at $4/user/mo undercuts it 7x on the seat line

Compute minutes burn faster than the headline number suggests - Windows and shared runners cost multiples of the base allowance, and a chatty test suite can eat 10,000 minutes in days (same trap as GitHub Actions, with a smaller allowance)

The tier walls are deliberate upsell levers: most security scanning, epics, portfolio management and compliance features live behind Ultimate, which is quote-only - mid-size companies get squeezed between 'not enough' and 'sales call required'

The AI billing story is a mess in transition: Duo Pro/Enterprise flat seats are being replaced by GitLab Credits usage billing with no published per-credit price, so budgeting AI spend means talking to sales
UI performance and review ergonomics lag GitHub - MR pages feel heavier, and code review culture on GitLab consistently draws complaints in team-migration retros

faq.question: Is the GitLab Free tier actually usable for a small team?
faq.answer: Yes, with a hard ceiling. You get 5 users per top-level group, 400 CI compute minutes a month, 10 GiB storage and unlimited private repos - fine for a side project or a 3-person shop that runs lean pipelines. The 400-minute allowance is the real constraint (GitHub's free tier gives 2,000), so anything with a real test suite will hit it. Small teams that self-host can sidestep runner limits entirely with their own runners, which cost nothing.

faq.question: How does GitLab's AI pricing work now that Duo Pro is gone?
faq.answer: GitLab moved AI features onto GitLab Credits, a usage-billing model: you prepay or draw down credits for Duo Agent Platform features like AI code review and agentic chat. Premium and Ultimate currently include promotional credits ($12 and $24 per user per month respectively) for a limited time, but GitLab does not publish a public per-credit price. Expect a sales conversation to pin down real AI costs - and check the promo terms before you model next year's budget, because the included credits are explicitly time-limited.

faq.question: Premium vs Ultimate - what is actually locked behind Ultimate?
faq.answer: The security and governance layer: dynamic and full application security testing, dependency and container scanning, fuzz testing, vulnerability management, license compliance, plus portfolio management and value-stream analytics. If your client needs compliance evidence (SOC 2, PCI, fed-style audits), you will end up on Ultimate. If they just need solid CI/CD, project management and priority support, Premium covers it. Get an Ultimate quote early - it is custom pricing and sales-quoted for a reason.

faq.question: Can we migrate off Jenkins to GitLab CI without stopping releases?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is the standard consulting engagement for this tool. Run both systems in parallel on the same repos, port one pipeline at a time starting with the least critical service, keep Jenkins as the fallback trigger until the GitLab pipeline has run green for a couple of sprints, then cut over. GitLab's include/extend template system makes pipelines 2 and 30 much cheaper than pipeline 1. Budget-wise, a mid-size org with a few dozen jobs usually lands between one and three months of parallel running.

features: Single DevSecOps application: repos, merge requests, CI/CD, container and package registries, environments and deployment wiring in one app
Advanced pipeline engine - parent-child and multi-project pipelines, DAG needs, shared CI templates via include, scheduled and merge-train pipelines
Security built in: SAST on every tier, plus DAST, dependency, container and license scanning, vulnerability dashboards and security policies on Ultimate
Duo Agent Platform (AI): code suggestions, AI code review, agentic chat, and on Premium/Ultimate the included Duo Core layer - billed through GitLab Credits usage
Deployment flexibility: run on gitlab.com, self-managed on your own servers, or GitLab Dedicated single-tenant SaaS
Value-stream and portfolio management on Ultimate: epics, roadmaps, cycle analytics and compliance frameworks
Granular permissions, protected branches and environments, push rules, and audit events for regulated teams
Free unlimited self-hosted runners - bring your own compute and the per-minute meter stops mattering
platform: Web UI at gitlab.com or your own self-managed instance (Linux package, Docker, Kubernetes); GitLab Dedicated for single-tenant SaaS; CI runners on Linux, Windows, macOS hosts you host or shared runners; CLI via glab; REST and GraphQL APIs; MCP server for AI-agent integration.
content:
GitLab is the platform teams pick when they want the whole software delivery chain - git hosting, code review, CI/CD, security scanning, deployment - inside one application instead of stitched together from five vendors. If GitHub Actions is the default because everyone is already on GitHub, GitLab is the deliberate choice: the one you make when a client says "self-hosted", "compliance", or "one throat to choke".

The comparison article on this site ([Best CI/CD Tools 2026](/articles/best-cicd-tools-2026-github-actions-vs-gitlab-vs-circleci-vs-jenkins/)) puts GitLab head-to-head with GitHub Actions, CircleCI and Jenkins - read that for the full bake-off. This page covers what GitLab actually costs in 2026 and where the money is for anyone selling DevOps work around it.

## What it actually does

The pitch is "a complete DevSecOps platform in a single application", and unlike most marketing lines, this one is literally true. A merge request in GitLab is also the place where CI pipelines report, security findings appear, review comments land, and deployments get gated. No webhooks to Jenkins, no separate SonarQube dashboard, no third-party artifact store unless you want one.

The CI engine is the strongest part. Parent-child pipelines let a monorepo spin up only the jobs that changed. Multi-project pipelines wire a deploy in one repo to a trigger in another. Shared templates through `include` mean a platform team writes the pipeline once and forty product teams extend it. DAG dependencies (`needs`) skip the artificial staging/waiting that YAML CI usually forces on you.

The AI layer is GitLab Duo, now delivered through the Duo Agent Platform: code suggestions in the IDE, AI code review on merge requests, and agentic chat for repo questions. Duo Core comes included with Premium and Ultimate; heavier usage draws down GitLab Credits. It is competent rather than spectacular - think "catches the missing null check and the N+1 query", not "writes your feature".

## Pricing: the real math

Verified against [about.gitlab.com/pricing](https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/) in October 2026:

| Tier | Price | Compute minutes/mo | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 400 | 5 users per top-level group, 10 GiB storage, SAST included |
| Premium | $29/user/mo (annual) | 10,000 | Unlimited users, advanced CI/CD, SLA mgmt, priority support, promo $12/user/mo credits |
| Ultimate | Custom quote | 50,000 | Full security scanning, compliance, portfolio mgmt, promo $24/user/mo credits |

Three things the sticker price hides:

1. **The seat math compounds.** Fifty developers on Premium is $17,400/yr - before a single AI credit is used. GitHub Team is $4/user/mo. You are paying the difference for self-managed hosting rights, built-in security scanning and the single-application model. Sometimes that trade is worth it; it should be a decision, not a default.
2. **AI billing is in flux.** The flat Duo Pro seat ($19/user/mo) is being replaced by GitLab Credits usage billing. Included credits on Premium/Ultimate are promotional and time-limited, and there is no public per-credit price. If AI spend matters to your budget, get a number from sales in writing.
3. **Compute minutes are not fungible.** Windows and shared runners cost multiples of the base allowance, same trap as GitHub Actions. The escape hatch is strong: self-hosted runners are free and unlimited on every tier, so a $30/month VPS can carry a workload that would otherwise burn thousands of minutes.

## The money angle: sell the pipelines, not the tool

GitLab has no meaningful affiliate program, and you should not want one. The margin is in the labor:

- **Jenkins → GitLab migrations.** The classic engagement. A mid-size org with dozens of Jenkins jobs pays $3,000-10,000 for a phased migration, and the deliverable is a template library that makes every future pipeline cheap. Jenkins expertise is aging out of the workforce faster than Jenkins is leaving datacenters - that gap is your market.
- **Managed DevOps retainers.** $1,500-5,000/mo per client to own the CI/CD setup: pipeline health, runner costs, dependency updates, deploy runbooks. Two or three retainers on top of a Premium self-managed instance is a real business.
- **Compliance builds.** Teams that need audit evidence need Ultimate features - security dashboards, policies, vulnerability management. Selling and configuring that stack is work generalist agencies can't do, which is exactly why it pays.
- **Runner economics consulting.** Sounds small, isn't. Moving a client from shared runners to self-hosted can cut their CI bill by 70-90%, and "I saved you $800/month" is the easiest retainer renewal conversation you will ever have.

The unglamorous truth: GitLab being paid software is an advantage here. Clients on free tools resist paying consultants; clients paying $29/seat already believe in spending money on tooling.

Once pipelines are healthy, observability is the next money conversation - our take on [DevOps monitoring tools](/articles/best-ai-devops-observability-tools-2026-datadog-vs-new-relic-vs-dynatrace-vs-splunk/) pairs well with a GitLab retainer pitch.

## Where it falls short

Honest list, because every migration project discovers at least two of these:

- **The tier walls are upsell architecture.** Most security scanning beyond SAST, plus epics, portfolio management and compliance features, sit behind quote-only Ultimate. Mid-size companies get squeezed between "not enough" and "talk to sales".
- **UI weight.** Merge request pages are slower than GitHub's, and code review ergonomics are the complaint that shows up in nearly every team migration retrospective. Plan on some grumbling.
- **Transition billing confusion.** The Duo seats → credits shift means two pricing models coexist in the docs right now. If you are writing a client proposal, double-check which model applies to their tier before you quote.
- **Free tier is tight.** Five users per top-level group and 400 minutes is leaner than GitHub's free tier (2,000 minutes). Fine for side projects, tight for anything with a real test suite.

## Who should pick it

Regulated teams, agencies and consultancies running client infrastructure, and any org that wants CI/CD, security and hosting under one roof with a self-managed escape hatch. If your code already lives on GitHub and your security story is "we'll add it later", GitHub Actions is cheaper and fine (we wrote a full page on [GitHub Actions](/tools/github-actions/) last week). GitLab earns its premium when self-hosting, compliance or the single-application model is a requirement, not a preference.

And if you sell DevOps work: the Jenkins-to-GitLab migration is one of the most repeatable, quoteable engagements in the market right now. Learn the template system properly - it is the difference between a $3,000 migration and a $10,000 one.

## FAQ

### Is the GitLab Free tier actually usable for a small team?

Yes, with a hard ceiling: 5 users per top-level group, 400 compute minutes a month, 10 GiB storage, unlimited private repos and SAST included. The 400-minute allowance is the constraint - GitHub's free tier gives 2,000 - so lean pipelines or self-hosted runners are mandatory for anything serious. For a 3-person shop that self-hosts runners, Free is genuinely enough.

### How does GitLab's AI pricing work now that Duo Pro is gone?

AI features moved to GitLab Credits usage billing. Premium and Ultimate currently include promotional credits ($12 and $24 per user per month respectively), time-limited, and the per-credit price is not published. Budget a sales conversation for AI costs, and read the promo terms before modeling next year's spend.

### Premium vs Ultimate - what is actually locked behind Ultimate?

The security and governance layer: DAST and full application security testing, dependency and container scanning, vulnerability management, license compliance, plus portfolio management and value-stream analytics. If a client needs audit-ready evidence, they need Ultimate. If they need strong CI/CD and priority support, Premium is enough. Get an Ultimate quote early since it is sales-priced.

### Can we migrate off Jenkins to GitLab CI without stopping releases?

Yes - run both systems in parallel, port one pipeline at a time starting with the least critical service, keep Jenkins as fallback until the GitLab pipeline runs green for a couple of sprints, then cut over. Shared `include` templates make pipelines 2 through 30 far cheaper than pipeline 1. Most mid-size orgs land between one and three months of parallel running.
